item.title: REVIEW: Parallels 27 review
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
Parallels has long been the best option for full Windows emulation on Macs and this is even more true in Parallels 27. While it is limited to Apple Silicon Macs and its best features require an annual subscription, improved graphics support with OpenGL 4.3 and AI functionality makes it the undisputed champion of VMs on MacOS. - +Easy installation of Windows and Linux - +Coherence mode allows seamless Windows app use - -Windows licensing adds to the overall cost - -Best features require annual subscription Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test. Apple offers some of the best workstations going, with everything from the MacBook Pro to Mac mini finding its die-hard adherents among professionals of all stripes, Sometimes, though, even the biggest Mac fans need to run software in a Windows environment, whether for software testing or you need to use a professional software suite that has no native Mac support. Enter Parallels 27, the latest version of the best virtual machine software that offers the best of both worlds for Apple users. This latest version of Parallels brings some big changes, including a complete rewriting of the graphics pipeline for the Apple Metal API, OpenGL 4.3 support (one of the most demanded updates among Parallels users), and the full move over to Apple Silicon-only. While that last bit might irk some who still cling to their Intel-based Macs, many more are going to take issue with the subscription-based model for its most in-demand features. Despite that, however, there’s no denying that Parallels 27 is the best way to host guest OSs on your Mac, and for most the pros are going to far outweigh the cons. Parallels 27 comes with four different plans for various use cases: Standard, Pro, Business, and Enterprise. The Standard plan is available as both an annual subscription and a one time purchase, with the annual subscription list price running $99.99 (about £75 / AU$145), while a one-time, perpetual license costs $219.99 (about £165 / AU$320). It should also be noted that the one-time purchase does not come with free upgrades to newer versions of Parallels, though the subscription plan does. For the Pro plan and above, an annual subscription is required, starting at $119.99 (about £90 / AU$175) for a Pro plan and $149.99 (about £110 / AU$220) for a Business plan. Enterprise customers will need to contact Parallels’ sales department to negotiate an Enterprise plan rate. For most casual users, the Standard plan is the way to go, though it is limited to four virtual CPU cores (vCPUs) and 8GB of virtual RAM (vRAM), though this should be more than enough for basic office software and productivity apps. Stepping up to the Pro tier or higher gets you up to 32 vCPUs and up to 128GB vRAM. The Pro plan comes with AI Agent Integration (MCP), disk and memory cleaner, system and performance monitoring, and screen capture and recording, among others. The Business plan includes those features, plus volume licensing with centralized license admin, automated CI/CD workflows for developers, and automated deployment and update support through Jamf and Intune integration. The Enterprise plan includes things like policy enforcement, compliance visibility, and many other IT tools for large businesses. The biggest sticking point for Parallels 27 is going to be these prices, largely because there are open-source alternatives out there, but they come with their own trade-offs that might not be worth the savings. None of this, by the way, includes the price of a Windows 11 license, and for businesses in particular, this expense can add up very quickly with multiple deployments across many Mac systems, but this would also be the case with open-source VMs. The biggest change to Parallels with version 27 is the end of Intel-powered Mac support. Parallels 27 was developed with macOS 27 in mind, and that OS update is Apple Silicon only, so Intel Macs will need to stick with Parallels 26 from here on out. Fortunately, Parallels will continue to support Parallels 26 with security and maintenance updates for some time at least. It’s also worth pointing out that Parallels 27 uses Windows on Arm by default, and this version of Microsoft’s OS has inherent Intel x86 app compatibility issues that Parallels can’t do anything about. There is an early technology preview allowing you to import existing Intel x86-based Windows VMs, but these will run significantly worse than a Windows on Arm VM since the entire instruction pipeline needs to be emulated. The other big change is the rewritten graphics driver for OpenGL 4.3 support based on Apple’s Metal API, one of the most requested features if Parallels support forums are any indication. A lot of professional software tools that are Windows-only (like ArcGIS Pro and various CAD software) use OpenGL 4.3, so earlier versions of Parallels struggled with these apps, if they were able to run at all. Parallels 27 is still capped at DirectX 11.1, however, so apps that require DX 12 won’t work. You also need to make sure you have the latest version of Parallels Tools installed to make sure that OpenGL 4.3 will work properly. Further, on Apple M4 systems or newer, there is now support for Apple’s Scalable Matrix Extension instructions in both Windows and Linux environments, which can speed up AI workloads in compatible apps. Beyond those changes, Parallels 27 retains the core features of earlier releases, with options to run the guest OS in a window on your macOS desktop, to have it use its own Space on you Mac, or to have individual apps work as-if-native through Parallels Coherence mode. There’s a shared folder between the host and guest OS to make file transferring simple, and drag-and-dropping from one desktop to another is seamless. The strongest argument in favor of Parallels, generally, is how low-lift setup and installation is. Unlike a lot of VMs out there, setting up the guest OS is as simple as a couple of button clicks and about 15 minutes of installation time. If you’ve never had to set up a VM before, I can assure you that this is arguably the easiest installation process you’re going to find on the market. You also have a lot of control over how many resources in terms of CPU cores and memory to assign to the VM, especially at the Pro tier and above, and these settings can be changes nearly on the fly if you need more performance (you do have to stop the VM first though, so save your work before doing so). Once everything is set up, Parallels feels like just another app on the Mac desktop, with your chosen guest OS running in a window you can click in and out of as needed. If you want a full screen desktop experience, you can get that too. Coherence mode is very useful if you need to work primarily in macOS but need occasional access to a Windows or Linux app for that work, but I’d argue that this isn’t the best reason to buy Parallels (Crossover does the same thing, by and large, and doesn’t require a whole operating system installation taking up memory and storage resources). The seamlessness of the overall experience can make you forget that you are using a guest OS, however, so if your organization handles sensitive data, whether from a legal/compliance perspective or internal policy, be sure to manage permissions properly as far as folder and clipboard sharing go, since separation is not the same thing as isolation. Fortunately Parallels has settings to restrict such sharing, but you will need to configure them appropriately for your specific requirements. The same is true with any VM, of course, but the ease of integration with Parallels is such that complacency might actually be a problem if you’re not careful. In a lot of ways, the complexity and foibles inherent to competing VMs make it harder to forget you are using a VM, and their more ragged interfacing actually helps keep you from oversharing. That simply isn’t the case with Parallels 27. Despite the ease of use, there are still going to be difficulties with some apps and setups that users might run into. Fortunately, for subscription customers at least, you do get phone, chat, and email support as long as your subscription is active to help diagnose any issues. Those with a bit more experience with VMs also have access to an extensive knowledge base covering everything from installations to device sharing and common configuration issues. There are also regular security and performance updates that subscription customers will have access to. There are things, however, that no amount of support is going to help with, particularly if you’re looking for Windows PC gaming support. DirectX 11 games and older should work well enough, but recent titles using DirectX 12 simply aren’t available, and no game is going to run nearly as well as they will natively, whether through a Mac-native version or running the game on a comparable Windows PC. For game devs (though understandably, this will be a very small subset of you), this latter point is important to keep in mind, and I would definitely recommend using an actual Windows PC for any build testing you need to do if you absolutely must code a game on a Mac. Of course, any time you are working with a virtual machine, you’re going to have to sacrifice some performance given the hardware restrictions. Performance is going to depend pretty heavily on what kind of CPU and memory allocations you make, so the higher you can afford, the better your experience will be. That said, even at the Standard plan’s four cores and 8GB memory restrictions, actual app performance is generally very good, though it will have much more limited multitasking capabilities. This is most obvious when comparing the same benchmarks across different configurations. In Cinebench R24 on a 10-vCPU/12GB-vRAM configuration on an Apple M6 chip, I was able to get a score of 184 for single core performance, which is more or less what you get with a 4-vCPU/8GB-vRAM configuration (TK). Its multi-core score drops with your allocated core count, however, from a 10-vCPU score of 999 in Cinebench R24 down to 601 with a 4-vCPU/8GB allocation. Similarly, in Geekbench 7, the 10-vCPU/12GB allocation netted a single-core score of 3,495, compared to the 4-vCPU/8GB allocation’s 3,417, which is only about 2% slower. Compare these to the native run of Geekbench 7, which scored 4,052, and you get at worst a roughly 16% hit to single-core performance with Parallels, which is genuinely pretty outstanding for a VM. The more limited configuration, however, came in with a roughly 31% lower multi-core score (10,356 to the 10-vCPU’s 15,044), and fares even worse next to the native score of 22,180, or about a 53% lower overall performance. This means that for single app use, you won’t see too much of a difference between a Standard and a Pro plan, but if you plan on doing a lot of work in Windows, including multitasking with several apps, the Pro plan is probably worth the investment. On the graphics front, the Parallels Display Adapter driver does a solid job, but its performance against native Mac apps is fairly underwhelming. Most of the graphics benchmarks I normally run, like 3DMark Steel Nomad and Solar Bay, won’t even run in Parallels, thanks to the lack of DirectX 12 support. In 3DMark Wild Life Extreme, meanwhile, a 10-vCPU/12GB configuration performed about 58% worse versus native Mac performance. In OpenGL testing, which is one of the bigger feature updates to parallels with this version, the Windows emulated environment performed somewhat better than the DirectX test, though the 10-vCPU/12GB allocation on an Apple M6 still performed about 31% worse in Unigine’s Valley benchmark (4,127 to 2,859). The Windows VM did manage to score slightly higher than native on Unigine’s Heaven benchmark, scoring 2,160 to the native runs’ average of 2,059, or about a 5% better showing. Parallels 27 doesn’t solve all of the compromises you need to make to run a Windows virtual machine on a Mac, but it comes pretty darn close. Its single-app performance running in Windows is nearly indistinguishable from its native counterparts (at least with most apps), and there’s no understating how easy it is to set up and use. Where it does stumble, particularly in multi-core performance necessary for the kind of multitasking you expect from a fully functional OS, is going to be highly dependent on the host system’s hardware. That said, it’s generally going to underperform what you can get using Mac-native versions of the same apps. But, if you were able to get those apps on a Mac, you wouldn’t be using Parallels, and so Parallels 27 offers as much of the best of both worlds as you are likely to find on the market.

item.title: SALES: Save 42% on MATEIN's Travel Laptop Backpack and simplify your holiday travel
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek
Holiday travel means keeping a laptop, your documents, and a pile of small items organized while you shuffle through crowded airports. A dedicated bag like the MATEIN Travel Laptop Backpack gives each of them a place to live. Right now, it's 42% off on Amazon, but only the Austere Grey color is at this price, and you need Amazon Prime to take advantage of the deal. - Polyester, nylon lining, metal zippers Matein's Travel Laptop Backpack does exactly what it says on the tin at a price point that's hard to complain about. Save on the MATEIN Travel Laptop Backpack The backpack fits laptops up to 15.6 inches in a compartment at the back, separate from the main section, so your computer is protected from jostling and kept separate from everything else. If you're hauling a rolling suitcase, the luggage pass-through strap lets you slide the backpack over the suitcase handle, so it rides on top of your luggage instead of weighing down on your shoulders. Storage comes down to two main compartments and six exterior pockets, so you can sort things by how often you need them. A soft pocket can hold glasses or a phone, a pen organizer corrals the small stuff, and a basic sleeve fits a tablet or Kindle. That layout works well when you want your laptop, a tablet, and everyday small items all within reach. A hidden stash pocket sits on the outside of your back, under the lower padding, giving you a spot for small valuables you'd rather keep close. You also get a soft top handle for quick lifts and a detachable key clip, so your keys don't get lost at the bottom of a compartment. The exterior USB port is useful during long layovers and also works as a pass-through. It connects to an internal cable that plugs into your own power bank. Once it's set up, you can charge your phone without opening the bag and moving everything around while you wait at the gate. Pair it with a power bank you already own, and your phone stays topped up between flights. But the MATEIN backpack isn't perfect. The bag has a flat bottom, so it won't stand up on its own, and there's no sternum strap to distribute weight more evenly. Those are fair trade-offs for a bag at this price, since the separate laptop compartment and luggage-strap handle take care of the jobs you'll care about most on a travel day. Overall, the MATEIN Travel Laptop Backpack is a practical pick for your holiday trips at a price that's currently under $20. Keep in mind that this price applies only to the Austere Grey color. The price has been fluctuating a bit over the last few days, so make sure to grab it before the price shoots back up.

item.title: REVIEW: Xbox Nano Controller Review: Somehow the Most Comfortable Portable Gamepad
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo
The Xbox Nano Controller is like a bright, funny, and exceptionally cute child split between parents going through the painful stages of divorce. It was built for another era of Xbox when the company still thought “Everything is an Xbox” was a tagline to get the crowds excited. That was an age when Microsoft imagined everybody would be keen to pay a monthly subscription to game on the cloud rather than on their Xbox or PC. When you're looking to avoid hand cramps on the go, the Xbox Nano is your best bet. Still, would it kill Xbox to give us Hall effect sticks? The $50 device has subtle capabilities that few modern controllers can claim. Unfortunately, you likely won’t end up using most of them. Instead, you’ll treat the Nano like you would any Xbox controller, just with a limited built-in battery that may not manage to match an entire extended flight from start to finish. The Nano controller takes inspiration from long-dead services like Stadia with the ability to play Xbox Cloud Gaming with relatively minimal latency via a direct Wi-Fi connection. But none of that actually matters all that much. This is now my favorite little travel controller, and it would be perfect if only it contained some amount of vibration or rumble to make gaming feel more immersive on the go. No, this isn’t what we should expect from future console hardware. It’s still potentially my favorite small-form-factor controller, if only for how well it fits into my massive, meaty claws. Out of all the companies making portable controllers, it’s Xbox that somehow crafted the one that’s most fine-tuned for adult-sized mitts. Don’t let the small stature and shape of the controller fool you; the Nano slips into my hands without any sense of cramping or button inaccessibility. With the miniaturized grips in the back, my middle fingers find a resting point on the plastic while the rest of my digits can close into a fist. I played several hours of Gears of War: E-Day and Star Wars: Galactic Racer this way, and after a few minutes I was playing without any sense that I was gripping such a small gamepad. The Nano contains two fully analog triggers rather than the clicky digital triggers you may be used to on a Nintendo Switch 2‘s Joy-Con 2 controllers. The action feels smooth, with a forceful springiness that’s especially pleasant for larger hands. Still, they don’t have the kind of travel you’d expect from a larger Xbox controller. This means it can be more difficult to feather the brake and throttle in a game like Forza Horizon 6 or get the perfect boost start in Galactic Racer. The A,B,X,Y button set has a thonky feel, though your partner may not enjoy the loud, hollow sound of each press while you’re both trying to relax in bed. The D-pad is also surprisingly sturdy. I miss the micro-switch directional pad of the larger Xbox controller, though I appreciate how they kept the same shape and feel on the Nano gamepad. In addition, Xbox included a single programmable button instead of the typical Share key. You can use the Xbox Accessories app on PC or Xbox Series consoles to set it for different actions, like a long press to take screen recordings on consoles or hit some other macro on PC. There’s nothing wrong with a bit of customizability. If I have one main complaint, it’s with the joysticks. They don’t feel terrible. They’re full-sized with grippy sides that keep my fingers locked in. They’re thinner than a typical Xbox gamepad, but I didn’t expect more from such a small controller. The main problem is that these are still using the age-old potentiometer stick design. That means the Nano is susceptible to stick drift, where wear and tear leads to inputs you didn’t intend during gameplay. This obsession with old-style sticks is just blatantly annoying. The pint-sized 8BitDo SN30, with its similar Xbox functionality and branding, uses Hall effect sticks that are more drift resistant. There are so many modern technologies that offer precise, drift-resistant controls, from TMR—available on Xbox-branded devices like the Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20—to even more modern capacitive sticks, like we’ve seen on devices like the Razer Prio fold-out mobile controller. No major console maker has yet to abandon the potentiometer, and the first one to do so will claim my kudos with a note that reads, “Took you long enough.” Is cloud streaming really your plan for mobile gaming? Xbox didn’t exactly sell the Nano Controller on the back of its cloud connectivity. In fact, it’s a feature that’s so hidden you have to look at the Xbox beta app on Android to find the feature. In essence, the controller works like an old Stadia controller that hooks up to the same Wi-Fi connection you’re streaming games from. This reduces input latency and leads to a cleaner gaming experience. It took me several attempts to get the Nano connected to my home Wi-Fi with the use of the Xbox beta app. Though multiple guides stated this feature is available through the Xbox accessories app, I couldn’t actually get my controller connected in that fashion. Still, it is an option for gamers still beholden to their Game Pass or Xbox Cloud Gaming subscription. It’s a shame then that Xbox is actively disuading users from jumping into cloud gaming. This month, Xbox instituted new hourly limitations for how long you’re able to game on the cloud each month. Those with base Game Pass Essential subscriptions can only game on the cloud for five hours each month. Premium subscribers get 10 hours, while Ultimate users can claim 15 hours. I know I’m lucky if I can spend 15 hours in front of my console between work and relationships, but I’d rather know I have access to my games whenever rather than be beholden to both my internet connection and Xbox’s restrictive clock limits. There are some other benefits to this controller’s Wi-Fi connectivity. You can update the firmware simply by loading up the Xbox Accessories app and downloading the update directly to the Nano; no need to source a USB-C cable. Otherwise, I would have preferred the controller include any semblance of rumble rather than pack a Wi-Fi chip inside. There’s another limitation for the Nano’s size and weight. A typical Xbox gamepad makes use of two AA batteries. Some gamers prefer this to the shorter lifespans of rechargeable batteries, though the Nano is packing a 500mAH battery inside. That’s enough to get you around five hours of constant game time. The controller charges rather quickly, and if you have access to a power cable, you can easily make it past the 50% mark from empty in under half an hour. Taken all together, I would have preferred something that feels more premium, with better sticks and a clickier D-pad. At the same time, I enjoy the feel of it so much this could become my number-one travel controller when I’m gaming on a laptop. I’m just waiting for Xbox to truly decide what it wants its company to be and then bring us a controller that will match up to our new expectations. Hopefully, the long-rumored Elite 3 isn’t as much of a hodgepodge as the Xbox Nano is.

item.title: REVIEW: Phison Pascari X201P 15.36TB SSD Review: Fast PCIe 5.0 write performance for AI and ingest servers
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware
Phison’s Pascari X201P meets its rated specs and pairs 12 GB/s sequential writes with a steady 600K random write IOPS, making short work of AI checkpoints. It gives ground at low and moderate queue depths, where QD1 writes and mixed workloads lag, and it ran warm on our bench. - -Mixed-workload performance trails at middle QDs Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test. Phison is serious about enterprise storage, and the Pascari X201P was not released lightly; it came in the night, under NDA, alongside this week’s Supercomputing 2026 event. The drive is part of the Performance X-Series, which handles intensive workloads where consistency is the name of the game. We were nevertheless pleasantly surprised by its write performance, with a steady 12 GB/s for sequential and over 600,000 random write IOPS, considering it’s marketed at the 1 drive write per day (DWPD) endurance point. Part of that surprise comes from the fact that this is Phison’s read-intensive PCIe 5.0 data center drive, a successor to the X200P. It comes in the U.2 form factor — which can be more convenient in many cases — from 1.92TB to 30.72TB, and an E3.S version from 3.84TB, in both single- and dual-port models. It stands next to its mixed-use sibling, the X201E, which is the one rated for 3 DWPD. What makes the X201P exciting, in part, is its own 16-channel X2 controller and the flash that’s inside. This drive is aimed at AI, analytics, and database servers, with its case made in the 4K 70/30 mix at higher queue depths. It passed Phison’s one-million-IOPS mark at QD128 in our testing of the 15.36TB model, and the drive met all of its rated specs, though its random read rating required polled I/O to reach on our bench. It faced challenges with QD1 writes, log commits, and the middle range of our mixed sweeps. Given its blend of performance, capacity, and endurance, we consider it a very competent entry from the company that was perhaps better known in the consumer SSD market until recently. The drive met or beat every rated performance figure that we can test, which should be the target of any enterprise SSD released today. If there’s an exception, it’s due to how we test; Phison lists a ceiling of 3,250K IOPS for 4K random read, which is higher than our bench allows with our interrupt-driven I/O, which we use rather than a polled approach. We also run a polled test on every drive for cases like this, and our result was 3,283K IOPS at the same queue depth Phison specifies, which shows the drive does exceed its specification. Phison Pascari X201P Features and Management Our sample is in the U.2 form factor, 15mm thick. We have the single-port SKU, ISE model XP208H0815T3P3216T310, with firmware X2WM6026. Some data we previously saw from the drive was reportedly on X2WM6025, but we confirmed X2WM6026 for all relevant results. We mounted the drive on a PCIe 5.0 x4 add-in card adapter for U.2, standing upright in the slot. Phison did not provide firm hardware details, but we were able to discover some things on our own. The flash was probably the easiest, as the company claimed it was a 321-layer part. That can only be SK hynix’s V9 TLC, which is not flash we’ve tested before in any product. It’s exceptionally fast and uses a three-deck design, which is relatively new for TLC flash. The flash could be credited with some of the exceptional performance measurements we see on the drive. As for the proprietary controller, we’ve heard that it’s using a combination of the standard Arm Cortex-R5 — these would be the main cores — with AndesCore RISC-V on the side. We’ve seen the latter before on the Phison E28 consumer SSD controller, which did have some enterprise-like aspects to it. The E28 is the newer design, built on a 6nm process with Andes’ newer N45 cores alongside the N25F, while the X2 is a 12nm part that, as far as we can tell, sticks with N25F-class co-processors. In this case, the X2 has twice the flash channels, which enables a superior level of performance out of TLC flash, as in enterprise you do not rely on pSLC. item.title: REVIEW: Acer Ovia T520 review: a fast, reliable mesh system with Wi-Fi 7 at a competitive price
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
The Acer Connect app could be clearer and more helpful for first-time users. However, we can’t fault the Wi-Fi performance of the Ovia T520, as it provides a wide-ranging and reliable mesh system with tri-band Wi-Fi 7 at an attractive price. Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test. The Acer Ovia T520 is a tri-band mesh router system running Wi-Fi 7. The Ovia range focuses on boosting range and reliability for larger homes and offices, in contrast to the Acer Predator line's focus on impressive performance for online gaming and streaming. The T520 doesn’t attempt to match the blistering speed of the Predator routers, but its top speed of 5.7Gbps should still be more than adequate for most home users and small businesses, and it can connect to up to 200 devices spread across thousands of square feet. It’s also competitively priced when compared to many rival Wi-Fi 7 mesh systems. Acer Ovia T520 review: Price & release date - How much does it cost? $199.99 / £149.99 - Where can you get it? Available in US, UK and EU The T520 is one of the more affordable mesh systems we’ve seen recently, providing Wi-Fi 7 and tri-band performance at a similar price to dual-band rivals such as the Netgear Orbi 373 or Amazon’s Eero 7. You can buy a single T520 and use it on its own as a conventional router for just $199.99 / £149.99, and Acer states that each router can cover an area of approximately 1200sq.ft. However, we tested a two-pack mesh-system that costs $379.99 in the US, and there’s a three-pack also available for $549.99. Customers in the UK get a good deal though, as the two-pack and three-pack systems are priced at £199.99 and £279.99 respectively. At the moment, the Ovia mesh systems are only available from Acer’s own online store, although they should be widely available from other online retailers in the US, UK and EU in the coming weeks. They are not currently available in Australia. The Ovia routers are neatly designed, looking rather like tall, white flower-pots. They’re fairly large, standing 202mm high and 116mm in diameter, and they house six internal antennae, so you’ll need a shelf or table with a fair amount of space when setting them up. They’re sturdily built, though, with cooling vents on the top and bottom panels, while the back of each router houses four 2.5Gbps Ethernet ports — one for your Internet connection (WAN), while the other three provide wired connections (LAN) for computers and other devices. Acer’s Connect app isn’t quite so straightforward, though. It doesn’t tell you which of the Ovia routers should be set up first and connected to your existing modem or router in order to use your broadband connection — as many of its rivals do — so people who haven’t used a mesh Wi-Fi system before might get confused here. Some of the instructions for connecting the second router were also confusing, such as the app telling me to wait for the LEDs on the routers to glow ‘solid white’ to confirm the connection – when in, fact, the lights were flashing green. By default, the app sets up two separate networks, reserving the fastest 6.0GHz frequency for newer computers and mobile devices that support Wi-Fi 7 or 6E. The slower 2.4GHz and 5.0GHz frequencies are combined into a single network to provide compatibility with older devices. However, that combined network was named ‘T520-2.4GHz’, which left me scanning through various menus within the app in order figure out what had happened to the 5.0GHz band. So Asus needs to make the app much more straightforward and provide clearer guidance for first-time users. As mentioned, the Ovia T520 provides tri-band Wi-Fi 7 with a top speed of 5.7Gbps, and that performance will handle gaming, streaming video and other demanding online tasks with no trouble at all. Again, though, it’s the Asus app that proves a little disappointing. The app does include basic features such as the ability to set up a guest network for visitors, as well as a Smart Home network that can be reserved for devices such as smart lights and security cameras. There’s also a QoS (quality of service) feature for managing the use of bandwidth on your network. But while many routers allow you to prioritize performance for specific tasks such as gaming or streaming, the Asus app requires you to laboriously specify the maximum speeds you want to allow for individual devices. It’s a similar story with the app’s parental controls. There is an option to create a schedule for Internet access so that the kids don’t stay up all night doom-scrolling on Instagram, but the automatic web content filters that we’ve seen with previous Asus routers weren’t available with the T520. Instead, the app requires you to manually set up a White List or Black List by typing in the addresses of individual websites — something that’s not exactly helpful for busy parents. Ookla Speed Test – 2.4GHz+5.0GHz (download/upload) Within 5ft, no obstructions: 150Mbps/150Mbps Within 30ft, three partition walls: 150Mbps/150Mbps Ookla Speed Test – 6.0GHz (download/upload) Within 30ft, three partition walls: 150Mbps Range and reliability can be a problem in many larger homes and offices, as evidenced by the Wi-Fi deadspot I have in a back office at the end of a hallway within my building. However, the two-piece Ovia system that I tested dealt with this problem effortlessly, with no need for a third mesh router either. Unsurprisingly the Ovia was able to take advantage of the full 150Mbps speed provided by my office network when connecting to nearby devices in the same room. Both of its networks — the dedicated 6.0GHz network and the combined 2.4GHz/5.0GHz network — breezed along at a consistent 150Mbps when running the Ookla Speed Test, and also when downloading large game files from Steam. The Wi-Fi connection also remained steady when I picked up my test laptop and walked along the corridor to that office at the back of the building, with both its networks maintaining a speed of 150Mbps for the Ookla and Steam tests. It’s not the fastest Wi-Fi 7 system currently available, but its speed of 5.7Gbps still outstrips most home broadband services and its competitive pricing makes the Ovia T520 a good option for any home or office that needs to improve the range and reliability of its Wi-Fi network. Should I buy the Acer Ovia T520? With two-pack and three-pack options available, the Ovia T520 is a good option for larger homes and offices that need to extend the range of their Wi-Fi network. The high-speed 6.0GHz band provides impressive performance, but you’ll need a recent PC or mobile devices that support Wi-Fi 6E or 7 to get the best performance. It’s competitively priced, but few homes will need the full speed of the T520, and there are many less expensive dual-band mesh systems available. We’ve seen routers from Acer that provide automatic content filters for blocking material that is unsuitable for children, but these are no longer available with the T520. The Orbi’s dual-band Wi-Fi 7 isn’t as fast as the tri-band Ovia, but its 3.6Gbps speed is still fine for gaming and streaming video, and Netgear’s app is much easier and more straightforward to use. Read our full Netgear Orbi 373 review. If speed is your main priority then Acer’s T7 provides blazing speeds of up to 11Gbps for gaming or streaming 4K video. However, it also has mesh capabilities so that you can use it as part of a mesh system as well. Read our full Acer Predator Connect T7 review.

item.title: REVIEW: Framework’s all-in-one keyboard wants to be the go-to pick for makers
item.description:
Source: PCWorld
Framework is one of my favorite PC makers thanks to its repair-friendly ethos and surprisingly open communication with customers. And I am, for my sins, PCWorld’s resident keyboard nut. So the moment I heard Framework was making a keyboard, my ears perked up like a dog that’s heard the can opener. Only to have them droop back down again. The Framework Keyboard is not mechanical, as I first assumed. But that doesn’t mean it’s bad, it’s just aiming for a different market. Specifically, the kind of market that needs a keyboard and mouse (touchpad) all in one device. The Framework Keyboard is a lot like the Logitech K400 and similar designs, ideal for PCs in odd places where a mouse won’t fit, like a home theater PC. Or indeed, the Steam Machine. Framework sent me a pre-production unit ahead of the planned Q1 release. The look is basic bordering on utilitarian, with slate-gray plastic, no backlighting, and only a device-switching button and a power toggle on top of the regular keyboard keys. The only splash of distinction comes from flipping the keyboard over, where you’ll see a smoke-transparent bottom housing that shows off its guts. That’s very cool, even if I would have preferred a splash of orange or purple. The lack of keyboard feet for an adjustable typing angle is significantly less cool, but I suppose this keyboard is intended to be used in a lap most of the time. And…yeah, that’s about it as far as the use case goes. It’s a standard wireless design with multi-device Bluetooth and dongle-based wireless. It has all the standard keys you’d find on a laptop board, plus a function row. It has no separate mouse buttons, the multi-point touchpad “clicks” instead. It’s a little wide because of the form factor…um, it has a USB-C port for charging or data? Yeah, I’m struggling to say much more about the physical design, because it’s just a keyboard with a touchpad. But if you thought Framework wouldn’t have something up its sleeve for its first input accessory design, you’ve got another thing coming. Like the company’s laptops and desktop, you can take this thing apart easily with a Torx screwdriver. Six little black screws are all that stand between you and the inside. From there you can unplug a ribbon cable, and it’s easy to see how the separate components like the battery, charging and control board, main keys, and touchpad can be replaced with a little more screwdriver work. That’s about all you can do with this repair-friendly approach, as there’s no real upgrades for these parts. But Framework does intend to sell these components individually, along with releasing Open CAD files, firmware, and schematics for all necessary parts. The idea is that the Framework Keyboard could become the de facto slim, laptop-style board for creators. This keyboard also works with the ZMK firmware system, a familiar interface for mechanical keyboard nerds. That makes it much easier to program than most regular keyboards, if they support that feature at all. Oh, one last cool thing: Framework sent me a “cradle” for the dongle, which fits into a standard Framework laptop or desktop modular USB-C port. With this extra adapter, the dongle sits flush with the case. Very cool, and something only Framework could do. It’s a separate purchase, and I haven’t been told how much yet. Here’s the downer: Framework plans to sell this board for $100 USD when it releases in early 2027. That’s not unreasonable for a repairable design with these components, especially considering its open nature. But it is about double what you’d pay for a similarly equipped combination board and touchpad, even from a major brand like Logitech. And though the keyboard Framework sent me is still a pre-production unit, its rather basic and mushy typing doesn’t make up the difference. Since it already has a steel backing, I can’t see this improving too much in a couple of months. If all you really need is a keyboard and touchpad for a PC or other gadget in a tricky spot, I don’t see a reason to pay double. The 3D printing folks might love it, and they already love Framework…but I think even they have cheaper options if they want these parts, not least of which are the parts that Framework already sells. I’d be a lot more enthusiastic about it if the price were knocked down 20 bucks or so. Framework’s Keyboard is up for pre-order now, with a refundable $50 deposit. It costs $100 in the U.S., $139 in Canada, €119 in the European Union, and £99 in the UK. Availability is “Q1 2027,” so you’ll have some time to work out if it’s worth the price for you or not.

item.title: SALES: The 100 Best Cheap Tech Gifts That Don’t Feel Cheap, Tested by Our Editors

Is your son's phone battery slowly dying? Have your friend's earbuds gone AWOL? If you're like most people with a holiday shopping list a mile long, you need thoughtful yet affordable options for the tech lovers in your life. But finding cheap, high-quality gear isn't easy, especially given volatile global markets and outrageous supply costs. Don't worry! We update this story monthly, so the values are always fresh. Go ahead and dig into our editor-curated picks to gift your friends and family some seriously cool tech while saving yourself some serious cash. Looking for the best of the best, regardless of price? Check the top products we've tested overall, as well as the latest winners of PCMag's Editors' Choice award. item.title: SALES: Grado's GW200 headphones boast fresh drivers and a longer battery life
item.description:
Source: Engadget
Grado's GW200 headphones boast fresh drivers and a longer battery life They run $329 and are up for preorder now. Grado has been a big name among audiophiles for decades. The company resisted making a wireless model until 2018 when it launched the well-received GW100 open-back headphones. Now, Grado is back with a major refresh of those initial Bluetooth cans. The GW200 brings a spate of upgraded features to the table. First of all, there's a newly-designed audio driver. The 44mm S is based on the larger drivers found with some of its wired headphones, like the HP100 SE. The company promises they delivery "clarity, detail and a full-bodied musical presentation while preserving the openness and natural character that define the Grado listening experience." The battery life here has also been improved. The GW100 headphones topped out at just 15 hours. This was an issue even back in 2018. However, the GW200 can last around 60 hours per charge, which is more in line with competitors. They can also operate via a wired 3.5mm connection and this won't draw any power. They use Bluetooth 5.4 and support for a bunch of common codecs, including Qualcomm aptX Lossless, aptX Adaptive and SBC, among others. The headphones also include multipoint connectivity that can maintain two simultaneous Bluetooth connections. That should make it easy to switch audio sources on the fly. These are on the lighter side, especially when compared to the GW100 headphones. The GW200 cans weigh 235 grams and include a padded leather strap and an adjustable steel band. They even integrate with the company's complete range of standalone headphone cushions, for increased comfort. Grado's new GW200 headphones are available to preorder right now and cost $329. Shipments should go out in December. Since launching the wireless GW100 headphones back in 2018, the company has also branched out into wireless earbuds.

In Villa de Ves, the night sky is reflected in the waters of a reservoir, while the Lagunas de Ruidera National Park, in the Sierra de Alcaraz and Campo de Montiel, offers a prime setting for observing the Milky Way at its 25 separate astronomical observation points. Further south, the Sierra del Segura range combines valleys, forests and quiet towns such as Riópar Viejo and Nerpio. In the Campos de Hellín, the southeast corner of the province, the lookout points at Agramón, Fuente-Álamo and Ontur invite you to gaze at the sky after exploring sites such as the Tolmo de Minateda (a rocky hill that was the site of Bronze Age settlements through to the Moorish occupation of Spain) and the Cancarix volcano. Two other stops to include on a La Mancha-Júcar itinerary are Villarrobledo and Villalgordo del Júcar. The former was established in the 13th century and is an important centre for Manchego cheese production; the latter is a picturesque town on the banks of the Júcar River. In the Monte Ibérico and Corredor de Almansa region, the countryside around Chinchilla de Montearagón and the Laguna Salada de Pétrola has spectacular landscapes that are particularly enchanting at sunset. CNT’s insider tip: Plan your getaway around the new moon to ensure maximum visibility at stargazing spots. Spend at least a few evenings away from the lights of towns and cities, wear warm clothing even if the forecast calls for a mild night and give your eyes time to adjust to the darkness. Why go: The southwestern corner of Andalusia is more than its endless beaches, quaint villages and picture-perfect sunsets. Here life moves at a different pace, and the local cuisine simply tastes better, from the shrimp fritters and fried fish to the sherry that accompanies them. There are many ways to enjoy the region at Spain's southern tip. There’s the maritime charm of Cádiz, its capital, with its narrow streets in the La Viña neighbourhood, its markets and La Caleta beach; the white villages of the mountains, with the towns of Vejer de la Frontera and Arcos de la Frontera standing out; and, of course, the Atlantic coast stretching from the beaches of Bolonia and Zahara de los Atunes to El Palmar. Then there is inland Cádiz, with the Sierra de Grazalema and many golf courses, and the marina at Sotogrande, one of the largest luxury developments in southern Europe. And there’s one more reason to visit in 2027. On 2nd August, the province of Cádiz will be one of the best places in Europe to witness a total solar eclipse. Clara Laguna CNT’s insider tip: You’ll want to choose the right time of year to explore Cádiz, depending on whether you love the heat or prefer milder winter months so you can do some more serious exploring without breaking into a sweat. And you’ll also want to check into some of the area’s new hotels. Recent additions include OKU Andalusia, in La Alcaidesa, the brand’s first family-friendly resort, with a spectacular kids’ club and an adults-only beach club; the Fairmont La Hacienda Costa del Sol, near Sotogrande, and the Amàre Beach Hotel Sancti Petri, south of Cádiz. The Royal Hideaway Sancti Petri has recently had its communal areas transformed by interior designer Jean Porsche while MiM Sotogrande, Leo Messi’s five-star boutique hotel, opened at the end of 2025. Why go: Those who have walked the Camino de Santiago in Galicia know that everyone should make this journey, which is both a literal and metaphorical adventure for many, at least once. It’s difficult to put into words the experience of walking the Camino de Santiago or even just to list all the emotions one experiences along the route that ends at the Plaza del Obradoiro in front of the cathedral in Santiago de Compostela. The first step in the journey is choosing which route to follow: The French Way, the Portuguese Way, the Original Way, the Northern Way or another route entirely. Whichever one you pick, they all lead to the wonders of Galicia. Once you’re there, you’ll be charmed by its villages, its unrivalled cuisine and a landscape that is impossibly, intensely green. Although the route’s original pilgrims were, of course, driven by their faith, today those who make the journey have a variety of motivations, but all are welcome regardless of what brings them to Spain’s northwestern corner. The year ahead promises to be particularly special as it is a Holy Year of St James (Ano Santo Xacobeo in Galician), a popular festival in Santiago de Compostela that takes place in those years when 25 July (the feast day of St James the Apostle) falls on a Sunday. Even though the number of pilgrims on the route increases considerably, it’s an even more exciting time to be part of the experience. CNT’s insider tip: The risk of rain on the Camino de Santiago is always high, which leads some people to prefer walking the route in the summer (temperatures are cooler here than in most of Spain), but we prefer the end of the peak season. In late September and early October, the landscape is a vibrant green, visitor numbers drop at least slightly and it’s a good way to delay the return to daily life that each autumn brings. One piece of advice when walking the route: Be prepared for unexpected emotional highs and enjoy every moment, even the ones that push you to your limits. Why go: The Ebro Delta, roughly halfway between Barcelona and Valencia, is one of the Mediterranean’s great natural paradises and a perfect destination for those who want to travel at a more leisurely pace in 2027. With its rice paddies, wild flamingos and pristine beaches, as well as colours that change with the seasons, ranging from greens and golds to earth tones and pinks, the Ebro Delta looks like it’s straight from a postcard. This birdwatching paradise is home to 350 identified species, but you don’t need to be an avian expert to enjoy the beauty of nature here. You can simply hop on a bike or take a stroll along Trabucador Beach and explore idyllic coves like those at L’Ametlla de Mar to be captivated by this watery world. On dry land, the medieval quarter and Gothic cathedral of Tortosa and fishing villages such as La Ràpita may end up being the highlights of your trip. The real luxury that the Ebro Delta offers is that of being able to switch off and disconnect, and some of its top accommodations will help you do exactly that. Villa Retiro in Xerta is a Modernista-inspired mansion dating from 1892, that has been converted into a hotel, complete with a swimming pool and a remarkable Michelin-starred dining experience. La Caseta in L’Ametlla de Mar is surrounded by olive trees and cooled by ocean breezes and the five-room Lo Hotel del Poblet is an intimate, adults-only option. There is also a new boutique hotel opening soon. We can’t share details yet, but we expect it will be the talk of Tarragona. Clara Laguna CNT’s insider tip: In addition to the natural wonders of the region, there are some culinary ones too. Rice dishes, oysters, mussels and fresh fish take centre stage in the Ebro Delta. Book a table at restaurants like Lo MUT at Mas Catxina, a boutique hotel surrounded by rice paddies, and Arròs i Brases, set in the gardens of the Tancat de Codorniu hotel. Why go: This magnificent Portuguese city is the European Capital of Culture for 2027. Évora, designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986, is home to monuments that span centuries. There’s an impressive Roman temple, a Gothic cathedral, an eerie Baroque chapel of bones within the Convent of São Francisco, the Royal Palace of Évora and many other architectural gems. Évora has more than enough reasons to make it worth a visit, but in 2027 it will add one more to the list when it assumes the title of one of the European Capitals of Culture. Even with the extra attention, we expect Portugal’s prettiest city will remain a peaceful place. If you visit outside the peak season or on a weekday, you can quietly stroll through its beautiful narrow streets without facing crowds of tourists. In addition to the cultural highlights, there are culinary ones too. Restaurants such as Tua Madre, A Cozinha do Paço and Forno da Telha introduce diners to recipes deeply rooted in the Alentejo region and its traditions. Don’t leave Évora without trying porco à alentejana (a stew of clams and pork), ensopado de borrego (lamb stew) and a dazzling variety of soups. And eat bread, lots of it, dipped in the region’s delicious olive oil. You should also raise a glass of wine produced on the herdades, farms scattered throughout the Alentejo, many of which now also double as hotels. After you’re done feasting, go for a stroll and embrace the philosophy at the heart of Alentejo culture. The motto for Évora’s period as a European Capital of Culture is “O Vagar é a cena,” or “Vagar is the thing,” with vagar being a concept that’s important in the Alentejo region. It emphasises valuing time and the relationship with oneself, with others and with nature. It reflects an ethos of coexistence, resilience and sustainability that fits Évora perfectly. David Moralejo CNT’s insider tip: Évora is situated halfway between the Atlantic and the Spanish border, roughly equidistant from the airports in Lisbon and Badajoz, Spain. In the heart of the Alentejo, the city has some magnificent hotels (Convento do Espinheiro, M’AR De AR Aqueduto, Imani Country House and Octant Évora), but it’s worth extending your trip to explore the surrounding region too. Here, you’ll find hotel gems such as São Lourenço do Barrocal in Monsaraz, which has just celebrated its 10th anniversary; the stunning Dá Licença in Estremoz; and, down on the coast, Vermelho by Christian Louboutin, RockRose and Pa.te.os in Melides, as well as Sublime Comporta and the long-awaited Na Praia (scheduled to open in 2027). All are located about an hour from Évora. Why go: Choosing between the different Canary Islands is not an easy task, but Fuerteventura is the perfect destination for anyone looking for adventure, water sports and miles of beaches. Every year, we could list endless reasons to visit any of the Canary Islands, but Fuerteventura makes our list for 2027 as it's looking better than ever. The island's well-known attractions, such as its desert landscapes; idyllic beaches like the 12-kilometre-long Cofete, the smaller La Concha with its turquoise waters, and the Bajo de la Burra beach with its unusual “popcorn sand”; and the famous Corralejo Dunes are now being complemented by a range of accommodation options that are putting the oldest island in the Canaries firmly on travellers’ radar. First came Paradisus by Meliá Fuerteventura, which was soon followed by Zel Fuerteventura. The two Meliá properties are right next to each other and together they form the Atlantic’s first wellness hub, where both resorts specialise in sport and wellness holidays, in keeping with the island’s identity. However, the best thing about them is their location right on Sotavento beach, one of the most famous in the area for its crystal-clear waters and white sand. The area, designated a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve, is also perfect for water sports, specifically windsurfing and kitesurfing. María Ángeles Cano CNT’s insider tip: Yes, Fuerteventura is famous for its idyllic beaches, but don’t forget to explore inland too. With its windmills and charming villages such as La Oliva, the area is worth a visit, and you’ll come across delightful projects like Casa Montelongo, a two-suite boutique hotel that’s a celebration of contemporary art and design. Avoid travelling during the windiest months, from May to August, when it can be difficult to enjoy the areas along the coast, and while all Canarian cuisine is award-worthy, you mustn’t leave without tasting the island’s traditional Majorero cheese. Why go: Perhaps the question shouldn’t be “why go?" but “why return?” since many of us already know that a single visit isn’t enough to take in the beauty of this Andalusian city. Whether it is a first visit or one of many, with the celebrated Federico García Lorca currently the focus of so much attention, it’s a fitting time to go to the city that is intimately associated with the poet and playwright. It’s easy to turn to Federico García Lorca for a description of Granada, since the poet often praised his city, but he was not alone. Many well-known figures, both from Spain and elsewhere, have been captivated by its charms. Alexandre Dumas, for example, once wrote: “I am beginning to think that there is a pleasure even greater than that of seeing Granada. And that is the pleasure of seeing it again.” The French novelist was certainly not wrong. What is it about this Andalusian city that so effortlessly charms visitors? There isn’t enough space to recount all its highlights, but perhaps it is the history that runs through the Albayzín neighbourhood, the authenticity of Sacromonte and its flamenco culture, the magic of the Paseo de los Tristes with its cafés and views of the Alhambra, the beauty of its cathedral and, of course, the impact that the Alhambra itself, the crown jewel of the city, continues to have on visitors who are left breathless at its beauty. It's an exciting time for Granada and one of its most famous locals in particular, Federico García Lorca, thanks to the success of the film La Bola Negra, which is selling out theatres around the world. It is also showcasing the beauty of the city in the best possible way by linking it to the works of a man who devoted his entire life to Granada. This is perhaps the perfect moment to understand the city through Lorca’s verses and surrender to its captivating allure. CNT’s insider tip: When it comes to accommodation, Granada has recently added another compelling reason to visit: the Gran Hotel Claridge. Located in the heart of the city, its location is unbeatable: from your room, you’ll feel like you can almost reach out and touch the cathedral. The rooftop terrace offers sweeping views of the Sierra Nevada and the Alhambra, as well as the cathedral. The Inizio restaurant, helmed by chef Rafael Arroyo, showcases the very best of Granada’s gastronomy. Its opening was one of the culinary highlights of the year in the city. Why go: The island’s 400 microclimates, flora and dramatic landscapes make it a place unlike any other in the world. Our correspondent in Portugal, Brais Suárez, wrote after visiting Madeira for the first time: “It’s not a particularly original observation, but it’s nonetheless fascinating that in the middle of the ocean several million years ago (which is not very long ago, apparently), a volcano erupted and spewed everything inside it out onto the surface. Like many other islands, this is how Madeira was formed. But, unlike most, the ferocity of the event can still be felt". The vertical walls of its basalt cliffs remind us of this moment with every kilometre we travel through this place with 400 microclimates and just as many different landscapes, as its inhabitants are fond of saying. To describe the fascination that Madeira holds in more detail might veer into overkill. We’ll just add that you might not yet know that it’s closer to the European mainland than the Canary Islands are, that figures such as the Empress Sissi and Winston Churchill visited here, and that Cristiano Ronaldo was born in its capital, Funchal (OK, perhaps you did know that one), and that its New Year’s Eve celebrations are magical with an almost endless display of fireworks. As for the food, you must try the delicious grilled limpets and the famous poncha cocktail (drink it in moderation—it goes down dangerously smoothly). David Moralejo CNT’s insider tip: When it comes to finding a place to sleep, the Savoy Signature hotels are a good place to start. The group, created by a local family, includes gems such as the Savoy Palace and The Reserve. Other excellent options include the legendary Reid’s Palace, A Belmond Hotel and the Hyatt Ziva Madeira resort. And make a note of the date 2 August 2027 when the eagerly awaited solar eclipse will be visible in Madeira, where 97% of the sun will be obscured. Why go: The recent opening of the Faro Santander museum is a reminder of the city’s unwavering commitment to art and culture. Santander, on Spain’s northern coast, is about much more than summer and squid, surfing and strolls along the oceanfront Paseo de Pereda, Sardinero Beach and the Magdalena Palace, once a summer home of Spain’s monarchs. In Santander, the year is drawing to a close with the opening of an exciting new arrival, the Faro Santander museum located in an iconic building on the Paseo de Pereda. The former Banco Santander headquarters has been revitalised by David Chipperfield, winner of the Pritzker Prize. It will host major temporary exhibitions that are transhistorical and cross-disciplinary. “The Botín Centre already has a well-established focus on contemporary art,” according to its director, Daniel Vega. In fact, the Botín Centre is just a short walk from the Faro, on the other side of the Pereda Gardens, allowing Santander to boast that it now has two exhibition centres of international significance. David Moralejo CNT’s insider tip: Although known as a summer resort destination, Santander doesn’t shut down in winter and it can more than hold its own against nearby Bilbao as a cultural destination. When it comes to where to stay on a visit, the Rhin Garden, recently refurbished by Sandra Tarruella, joins the city’s classic hotels such as the Eurostars Hotel Real, the Gran Hotel Sardinero and the Chiqui. The former Central and Paris hotels, once iconic properties, are both currently undergoing complete transformations ahead of their re-openings. In fact, the old Paris building has been demolished, and a replica is being built, adhering to heritage requirements. Why go: In 2027, an exhibition will examine the works of Francisco Goya (who trained in Zaragoza before moving to Madrid), and his influence on later painters from Manet to Picasso. Zaragoza, the capital of Aragon in northeastern Spain, has a number of nicknames: The City of the Wind, The Immortal City, The City that Never Gives Up. Its residents are more than happy to explain the stories behind those epithets, perhaps over hot chocolate and churros at La Fama or while perusing the stalls at the Central Market. Later you may want to take a walk across the River Ebro. The city doesn’t lack sights to see or things to do. You can start at the Plaza del Pilar and then step inside the enormous Baroque Cathedral-Basilica of Our Lady of El Pilar where the sunlight streaming through its windows and oculus will guide you towards the high altarpiece, Goya’s frescoes and the Holy Chapel. Pick up an Our Lady of El Pilar ribbon, an amulet and popular souvenir from Zaragoza. Continue on to La Seo (which is a co-cathedral along with the basilica; Pope Clement X’s solution in 1676 to the rivalry between the two churches), the Museo del Foro, the Roman walls, the Aljafería Palace, the Puerta del Carmen and the Patio de la Infanta. In 2027, from 16 April to 8 August, the Lonja de Zaragoza exhibition space will host Two Hundred Years with Goya, featuring around a hundred works that will showcase his influence on later artists including Manet, Picasso and Robert Rauschenberg. Among the works on loan from the Prado will be The Colossus, which returns to Zaragoza for the first time in more than 30 years. After you’ve had your fill of culture, do as the locals do and get a vermouth. Head to El Tubo, a neighbourhood that is the city’s gastronomic heart, and start the evening with a mushroom tapa at El Champi. You’ll want to leave room for the vegetables at Casa Lac and the roast lamb at El Fuelle. If you’re in the mood for a tasting menu, in this UNESCO Creative City of Gastronomy, La Prensa and Gente Rara (both Michelin-starred) and Gamberro take Aragonese cuisine in unexpected directions. The José Antonio Labordeta Parque Grande and the banks of the Ebro invite you to explore a different side of Zaragoza, one that helped to earn it the title of European Green Capital for 2028. When evening falls, cross the Puente de Piedra to the Balcón de San Lázaro. There you’ll see the Basilica of El Pilar again, now with its towers and domes bathed in the evening light. If the strong and cold cierzo wind is blowing, hang in there as any good resident of Zaragoza would. They are good people who are loyal, a bit stubborn and proud of their city and their refusal to be deterred by something as inconsequential as the weather has a long history. María Casbas CNT’s insider tip: Come in spring for the feast of San Jorge (Zaragoza’s patron saint) on 23 April or Zaragoza Florece, a flower festival in late May. In summer, make the most of the new flight connections planned for 2027 (the airport is scheduled to almost double the number of destinations it serves). In autumn, the Jazz and Film festivals are cultural highlights. At Christmas, there’s a giant nativity scene and ice rink on the Plaza del Pilar. Finally, on 12 October each year thousands of faithful, each one bearing a bouquet, create a vast mantle for the Virgin during the Offering of Flowers, a stunning spectacle. This story was originally published by Condé Nast Traveler Spain. It was translated by John Newton.

item.title: SALES: The Best Resorts in Turks and Caicos: Readers’ Choice Awards 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
Trends come and go, but here at Condé Nast Traveler, one thing never changes: your insatiable appetite for seeing the world. This year our readers cast an almighty 798,867 votes in our 39th Readers’ Choice Awards to tell us about the planet’s best travel experiences: You fell hard for palace hotels in Morocco, cruised down the Amazon, and got swept up in New York City’s exhilarating energy. Now, read on to find out where your favorites fall among the winners—and get inspired for where to go next, whether it's to a top-rated hotel or resort, or centered around a worthy cruise, spa, or island. These are the best hotels in the world as voted by you, our readers. - Read Full ReviewTurks and Caicos’s bustling yet beautiful island of Providenciales (affectionately dubbed “Provo”) has had its moment in the proverbial sun. Consider venturing southeast to South Caicos for a more intimate and undeveloped look at what are arguably the Caribbean’s most jaw-dropping beaches. The first property to put down literal roots with nearly 800 acres of primarily local vegetation is Sailrock South Caicos: a stunning, 40-unit property on the southeastern island’s northern tip where the Atlantic Ocean and Caicos Bank converge to house the area’s latest and greatest escape. Travel to South Caicos is also more convenient than ever with two direct flights from Miami on Wednesdays and Sundays via American Airlines. This means guests can now bypass a layover in Providenciales and reach paradise in less than two hours. - Read Full ReviewAt the Ritz-Carlton Turks and Caicos, guests can sandwich sun-soaked days of lounging in a private cabana or on Grace Bay’s idyllic slice of beach with plenty of on-site experiences. A favorite for its white-sand beachfront and unrivaled centrality on famed Grace Bay, there’s no shortage of pursuits here—it’s a choose-your-own-adventure property with great amenities for young kids. 147 luxury ocean-view rooms and suites—with the Ritz-Carlton standard—awe and delight. There’s also a collection of luxury residences and penthouses for longer stays, each, of course, with stunning floor-to-ceiling views of Grace Bay’s turquoise waters. Interiors are all creams and whites with gentle pops of beachy colors, large windows, and pristine linens. As the most central property in Grace Bay, everything is within walking distance: the best restaurants, shops, and even a grocery store. For families with little ones, the Ritz Kids club is the place to be for guests ages 4–12. Drop the kids off and embark on the resort’s luxury sailing catamaran, the Lady Grace. - Read Full ReviewSalterra balances solitude and serenity with grace. Backgrounding the sprawling complex is a skirt of rugged cliffs and leafy tropical flora—the stuff of our beach getaway daydreams. With staff-organized excursions across the gin-clear Caribbean, a seaside garden sprinkled with lounge chairs begging for sunbathers, and a state-of-the-art spa with eight treatment rooms, whether you're up for an adventure or down for a little R&R, the choice is truly yours. While the island is only home to 1,100 total residents, guests in search of an even greater sense of privacy can book private cabanas looking over the four sun-lit pools that bleed into the horizon. - Read Full ReviewBasking on a coveted stretch of Grace Bay, this well-appointed resort is as lax as it is luxe. While there’s plenty of opportunities for R&R at the blissful on-site spa and for romance to blossom over candlelit dinners, the Sands at Grace Bay also know a thing or two about picking up speed. It wouldn’t be a proper Turks and Caicos vacation without hitting the water, and the resort provides complimentary access to a variety of water sport equipment ranging from sea kayaks to snorkeling gear to explore the mirror-clear seas. If you’re traveling with little ones who aren’t quite ready for the open ocean yet, there’s also kid-friendly pools and sprawling perfect for their next adventure. If you’re looking for a resort that grows up alongside your family, look no further. - Read Full ReviewWymara Resort + Villas sits on the western curve of Grace Bay in Providenciales, just a 10-minute drive from the airport. It’s a place for travelers who like their luxury understated and favor the clean lines of minimalist design. Rooms and suites open to sea views and sun-washed balconies, while the villas—set apart from the main resort on a 15-acre peninsula—offer private pools, over-water decks, and personal hosts. The food is sustainably sourced: Indigo serves refined Caribbean dishes, and the Pink Bar is a magnet for sunset watchers. The spa, using island-grown botanicals and 111SKIN products, is intimate and calm. Service is polished yet relaxed, with staff who are friendly and will remember your preferences. Eco credentials are strong, from solar-powered electricity to refillable amenities. Complimentary wellness activities include yoga, pilates, HIIT, and sound baths, while evening entertainment leans local and cultural. - Read Full ReviewThis mega-resort sets itself apart from other all-inclusive properties throughout the region with its family-friendly activities. There is a 45,000-square-foot waterpark and kids clubs for different ages, including one with Caribbean-ified Sesame Street characters, the Xbox Play Lounge, and a teen disco. For the rest of the family, there are 10 swimming pools, 21 restaurants, 15 bars (some of them swim-up), and access to the 12-mile Grace Bay Beach. The 758 rooms and suites are spread across five themed villages, with architecture that represents different regions: France, Italy, the Caribbean, and Key West. With 43 room categories, the resort truly offers something for everyone. - Read Full ReviewGrace Bay Club offers not one, but three distinct accommodations to its discerning guests: the adults-only Hotel building, the family-friendly Villas Suites, and the Estate, a resort within a resort, with exclusive access to dedicated amenities, such as a separate pool, cabanas, and more. Despite catering to different crowds, they do have a few common features, including spectacular oceanfront views and personal concierge service. Head to the oceanfront Infiniti Restaurant & Bar for bites of such fresh local fare as a warm South Caicos lobster salad, garnished with shaved carrots and crispy basil, or the Mahi Mahi carpaccio, with a kick of jalapeño, served to the sound of breaking waves. Looking to stake your umbrella in the sand a little while longer? Rent one of the homes in the Private Villa Collection, a cluster of five freestanding private beachfront residences that come with all the amenities and services of a superior hotel stay, including roundtrip airport transfers, daily housekeeping, and complimentary breakfast. - Read Full ReviewA fan-shaped trio of seven-story buildings curve around a beachfront pool and patio at this Grace Bay resort, close to Providenciales's shopping district. Enormous rooms in soft colors have marble baths and soaking tubs, proving that bigger can mean better. Staff members always serve with a smile and make a point of remembering names. The restaurant Seven dishes up Caribbean-inspired cuisine, with entrees like house-made stone crab ravioli, or you can opt for private beachfront dining, complete with a personal butler and a playlist of your choosing. If you're traveling with the family, the kids camp provides diversions such as lizard hunting and sand-castle building—or you can all go for a dip in the island's only heated saltwater pool.
